warmup.question: To start us off, tell me a little about yourself.
warmup.answer: I recently finished a computer science degree and did an internship building backend services in Python. I'm looking for my first full-time engineering role.

questions.question: Describe a time you disagreed with a teammate about how to do something. How did you handle it?
answers: I don't really disagree with people because usually I'm right. When a teammate had a different idea I just did it my way and showed them later that mine was better.

In a university group project my teammate wanted to use MongoDB and I thought a relational database fit our data better because we had a lot of relations. We each explained our reasons in a meeting and I listened to his concern about flexible schemas. We agreed to use PostgreSQL with a JSON column for the flexible parts, and it worked well for the project.
followups: You said you're usually right. Walk me through how you knew that in that situation.
Looking back, when you said you're usually right, what did your teammate see that you might have missed?

signals.text: Specific example with the nature of the disagreement
signals.quote: teammate wanted to use MongoDB and I thought a relational database fit our data better

signals.text: Listened to the other view; focused on the problem, not the person
signals.quote: I listened to his concern about flexible schemas

signals.text: Used data/prototype/third opinion or compromise
signals.quote: We agreed to use PostgreSQL with a JSON column for the flexible parts

signals.text: Outcome and relationship preserved; reflection

red_flags_hit.quote: I don't really disagree with people because usually I'm right.

strengths: You gave a concrete technical disagreement (MongoDB vs relational) with reasons on both sides.
You listened to your teammate's schema-flexibility concern.
You reached a compromise (PostgreSQL with a JSON column) that worked.

gaps.what_a_stronger_answer_adds: Say what you learned or would do differently, and that the working relationship stayed good.
Back the decision with evidence, such as a quick prototype or a data-model comparison.
Drop the 'I'm usually right' framing and the 'did it my way' habit, which undercut your collaboration.

questions.question: You led a team of 4 using Git feature branches and pull request reviews on GitHub. What's the difference between git merge and git rebase, and when would you prefer one over the other when integrating those branches?
answers: They are basically the same thing with different names. If rebase gives an error I just force push to main and it fixes everything.

Merge takes two branches and combines them with a merge commit, so the history shows that they diverged and came back together. Rebase takes my commits and replays them on top of the other branch so the history is a straight line. I like to rebase my feature branch onto main before opening a pull request to keep history clean, and I use merge when I want to keep the exact history.
followups: When you say they're basically the same, how would you explain to a teammate what happens differently between them?
Could you explain in your own words what a force push to main does to your teammates' copies of that branch?

signals.text: Merge combines histories with a merge commit; preserves true history
signals.quote: combines them with a merge commit, so the history shows that they diverged

signals.text: Rebase replays commits on top of another base, giving linear history and rewriting commits
signals.quote: replays them on top of the other branch so the history is a straight line

signals.text: Do not rebase shared/public branches
Stated preference with reasoning (e.g. rebase local feature branch before PR)
signals.quote: I like to rebase my feature branch onto main before opening a pull request

red_flags_hit.flag: Says rebase and merge are the same
red_flags_hit.quote: They are basically the same thing with different names.

red_flags_hit.flag: Recommends force-pushing rebased shared branches without caution
red_flags_hit.quote: I just force push to main and it fixes everything.

strengths: You correctly explained that merge creates a merge commit and keeps the diverge-and-rejoin history.
You correctly described rebase as replaying commits onto another base, giving linear history.
You gave a sensible preference: rebase a feature branch before a PR, merge to keep exact history.

gaps.what_a_stronger_answer_adds: State the golden rule: never rebase shared branches, since rewritten SHAs cause conflicts for teammates.
Say that rebase rewrites commits into new SHAs, which is why force-pushing is risky.

questions.question: You mentioned adding a Redis cache to bring the orders API response time from 800 ms to 350 ms. Redis stores data as key-value pairs, so when would you choose a hash map over a list, and what are the trade-offs?
answers: A hash map keeps everything sorted so searching is O(log n) like binary search. You should always use it instead of a list because it is better in every way.

I'd use a dictionary when I need to look things up by a key. A hash map computes a hash of the key and jumps to a bucket, so lookup and insert are O(1) on average, whereas finding a value in a list means scanning it, O(n). A typical case is counting word frequencies or caching results by id. The trade-offs are that keys have to be hashable and unique, it uses more memory than a list, and in the worst case with lots of collisions it degrades toward O(n). Also it's not sorted by key, so if I need ordered range queries I'd use a sorted structure instead.
followups: Could you walk me through that in a bit more detail, ideally with a concrete example?
Earlier you said it is better in every way. What makes you say that?

questions.question: What is the difference between inheritance and composition? When would you prefer composition?
answers: Inheritance is for reusing code and composition is for combining classes. Composition is better because inheritance is bad in general and you should avoid it.

Inheritance is an is-a relationship, a Dog is an Animal, and composition is has-a, a Car has an Engine. Inheritance couples the subclass tightly to the parent so changes in the base class can break children, and deep hierarchies get hard to reason about. With composition I hold the collaborators as fields and can swap them, which also makes testing easier because I can pass a fake Engine. I'd still use inheritance when there's a real is-a relationship with shared behavior and the subtype can be substituted anywhere the parent is used, like different payment providers behind one interface.
followups: When you say inheritance is bad in general, what's your reasoning behind that?
What's a downside of composition compared with inheritance that you'd have to manage?

signals.text: Inheritance is an 'is-a' relationship; composition is 'has-a'
signals.quote: composition is has-a, a Car has an Engine

signals.text: Inheritance couples subclass tightly to parent; composition is more flexible
signals.quote: Inheritance couples the subclass tightly to the parent

signals.text: Concrete example (e.g. Car has an Engine; avoid deep hierarchies)
Mentions 'favor composition over inheritance' or testability/substitution
signals.quote: which also makes testing easier because I can pass a fake Engine

strengths: You correctly defined is-a vs has-a with the Dog/Animal and Car/Engine examples.
You explained tight coupling, base-class changes breaking children, and the testing benefit of swapping fakes.
You said when inheritance still fits: true substitutability, like payment providers behind an interface.

gaps.what_a_stronger_answer_adds: Name the principle 'favor composition over inheritance' explicitly, and avoid the blanket first claim that inheritance is bad.

questions.question: You mention fixing a production bug where duplicate orders were created when users double-clicked submit. Tell me about a mistake you made in a project or at school, perhaps like this one. What happened, and what did you do about it?
answers: I can't think of any big mistake. If I have to say a weakness, I work too hard and care too much about perfection.

During my internship I ran a migration script against the staging database without checking the environment variable and it was actually pointing at the shared QA database, so I deleted a day of test data other testers were using. I told my lead right away instead of hoping nobody would notice, restored the data from the nightly backup within an hour, and messaged the testers about what happened. Afterwards I added a confirmation prompt that prints the target host before any destructive script runs, and proposed that we color-code the QA prompt differently.
followups: You said you can't think of any big mistake. What makes you feel that way? Tell me in your own words.
Looking back, what habit did you change in how you run scripts against shared environments, beyond the prompt you added?

signals.text: Specific, real mistake with real consequence
signals.quote: deleted a day of test data other testers were using

signals.text: Takes ownership without excuses
signals.quote: ran a migration script against the staging database without checking the environment variable

signals.text: Fixed it and communicated to affected people
signals.quote: restored the data from the nightly backup within an hour, and messaged the testers

signals.text: Process change to prevent recurrence
signals.quote: added a confirmation prompt that prints the target host before any destructive script runs

red_flags_hit.flag: Claims no mistakes, or a fake-weakness answer ('I work too hard')
red_flags_hit.quote: I work too hard and care too much about perfection

strengths: You told your lead right away instead of hiding the mistake.
You restored the data and told the affected testers what happened.
You added a concrete safeguard: a confirmation prompt showing the target host.

gaps.what_a_stronger_answer_adds: Say whether the team adopted the color-coding proposal and how the safeguard was checked.
